item.title: Van Gogh's 'The Starry Night' depicts the sky on July 22, 1889, researchers find
item.description: null Researchers think they might have pinpointed the exact night sky that we see depicted in Vincent van Gogh's iconic painting "The Starry Night." Perhaps one of the most famous paintings in modern history, Van Gogh's "The Starry Night" carries a legacy that continues to inspire and mystify generation after generation. But while you might see in its swirls of color and bright spots of starlight a night sky derived purely from imagination, some scientists think it represents an actual view — one that includes a waning crescent moon, Venus and the Hyades cluster. And they may know exactly when this sky appeared.. In a new study, researchers suggest that "The Starry Night" depicts the pre-dawn sky seen around July 22, 1889 from Saint-Rémy-de-Provence, where Van Gogh painted it. But while this sky happens to perfectly match the one depicted in the artwork, art historians have long thought that Van Gogh painted this piece in June. Could these findings shift the date of this legendary artwork? Finding a painted sky This investigation started decades ago with art historian Albert Boime and astronomer George Abell at UCLA in 1984 and continued in the following years with astronomer Charles Whitney at Harvard University. However, these earlier analyses did not agree with one another, and there was no true consensus about exactly when the sky matched with the painting. So the question remained, lingering in the minds of those with a shared love for both art and space. And a team led by Elijah Jeong-hyun Kim, the CEO of South Korean robotic telescope company SLLAB and a Ph.D. candidate at Kyung Hee University's School of Space Research, picked up the search once more. "When they see a fragment of a starry sky, observational astronomers like me and amateur astronomers alike will want to solve the puzzle. I am simply someone who pursued that process a little more actively," Kim told Space.com . A figure from Kim et al.'s paper in Scientific Reports. According to the figure: "The central cluster of stars in The Starry Night (1889), left, and the Hyades cluster in Taurus, center. At right, the five stars in the painting (orange) are overlaid on the real stars (blue) after matching for size, orientation and position; red dashed lines show the residual differences." (Image credit: Kim et al., Scientific Reports (2026)) But how did Kim's team come to their conclusion, after others had failed to nail down a date over the decades? In short, "we analyzed the painting astronomically, analyzed documents about his situation in July 1889, and then carried out ecological and meteorological investigations," Kim said. To start with, the team analyzed the sky from the exact location in Saint-Rémy where Van Gogh is said to have painted "The Starry Night." They then used observational geometry to map the historical night sky. item.dc:creator: Chelsea Gohd
item.content:encoded: null Researchers think they might have pinpointed the exact night sky that we see depicted in Vincent van Gogh's iconic painting "The Starry Night." Perhaps one of the most famous paintings in modern history, Van Gogh's "The Starry Night" carries a legacy that continues to inspire and mystify generation after generation. But while you might see in its swirls of color and bright spots of starlight a night sky derived purely from imagination, some scientists think it represents an actual view — one that includes a waning crescent moon, Venus and the Hyades cluster. And they may know exactly when this sky appeared.. In a new study, researchers suggest that "The Starry Night" depicts the pre-dawn sky seen around July 22, 1889 from Saint-Rémy-de-Provence, where Van Gogh painted it. But while this sky happens to perfectly match the one depicted in the artwork, art historians have long thought that Van Gogh painted this piece in June. Could these findings shift the date of this legendary artwork? Finding a painted sky This investigation started decades ago with art historian Albert Boime and astronomer George Abell at UCLA in 1984 and continued in the following years with astronomer Charles Whitney at Harvard University. However, these earlier analyses did not agree with one another, and there was no true consensus about exactly when the sky matched with the painting. So the question remained, lingering in the minds of those with a shared love for both art and space. And a team led by Elijah Jeong-hyun Kim, the CEO of South Korean robotic telescope company SLLAB and a Ph.D. candidate at Kyung Hee University's School of Space Research, picked up the search once more. "When they see a fragment of a starry sky, observational astronomers like me and amateur astronomers alike will want to solve the puzzle. I am simply someone who pursued that process a little more actively," Kim told Space.com . A figure from Kim et al.'s paper in Scientific Reports. According to the figure: "The central cluster of stars in The Starry Night (1889), left, and the Hyades cluster in Taurus, center. At right, the five stars in the painting (orange) are overlaid on the real stars (blue) after matching for size, orientation and position; red dashed lines show the residual differences." (Image credit: Kim et al., Scientific Reports (2026)) But how did Kim's team come to their conclusion, after others had failed to nail down a date over the decades? In short, "we analyzed the painting astronomically, analyzed documents about his situation in July 1889, and then carried out ecological and meteorological investigations," Kim said. To start with, the team analyzed the sky from the exact location in Saint-Rémy where Van Gogh is said to have painted "The Starry Night." They then used observational geometry to map the historical night sky. "Modern telescopes are equipped with a function called astrometry, which compares an image of the night sky with celestial coordinates stored in a computer and automatically extracts the coordinates of the image," Kim said. "We used Procrustes analysis, a method that compares only the 'shape' of two sets of points. After matching their position, size and rotation, it measures how similar the two shapes are from the differences that remain (the residuals)." "Because a star cluster on the canvas may be larger or smaller than in reality and slightly tilted, this method was the right fit. It allowed us to explain, in quantitative terms, what earlier studies had described only qualitatively as 'resembling a certain constellation,'" Kim added. But this quantitative analysis wasn't enough to say for sure that this was the right-fitting sky, as different constellations could fit to a similar degree, Kim explained. To get closer to their answer, the team combined their analysis with a deep dive through history. "We also checked whether the stars were actually in that part of the pre-dawn sky on that date, whether they fall within the painter’s field of view, and whether the appearance of the moon and Venus matches the painting. It was the Hyades that satisfied all of these conditions," Kim said. Exploring astro-art history As mentioned, the date of this matching sky comes in late July, a month after art historians think Van Gogh painted "The Starry Night." But the researchers suggest that their findings could provide evidence to support the idea that the work was actually painted in July. Letters written by Van Gogh as early as 1888 describe his desire to paint a star-filled sky. A letter dated April 12, 1888 reads: "A starry sky, for example, well — it’s a thing that I’d like to try to do, just as in the daytime I’ll try to paint a green meadow studded with dandelions." Kim followed these letters through the months to try and find more information that could potentially alleviate the discrepancy between the matching skies and the actual month the painting was created. Kim pointed to a letter from between late May and early June 1889 that reads: "This morning I saw the countryside from my window a long time before sunrise with nothing but the morning star, which looked very big." Kim drew on "personal imagination" to find ties between Van Gogh's sky observations in these months and what they might mean for the painting's timeline, Kim shared, so this doesn't definitively change the view of this painting's history. However, Kim suggested that these records could indicate that Van Gogh was repeatedly looking up and watching the pre-dawn sky, which could have led to him seeing this exact sky on July 22. The painting itself even ignites uncertainty among art historians. As the researchers cite in their new paper, leading art historians see "The Starry Night" as stylistically different from Van Gogh's other works during the month of June, drawing further questions over the date painted. "What our study shows is that the sky in the painting matches, in both observation and shape, the real pre-dawn sky around July 22. So, what we propose is the possibility that Vincent conceived the idea in June and completed the painting after July 22," Kim said. However, "I think further research in art history and conservation science could shed more light on this question," Kim added. This work was described in a study published Oct. 22 in the journal Scientific Reports.

item.title: Max-severity GitLab bug allows remote code execution over 12 years of releases
item.description: GitLab on Wednesday patched a maximum-severity flaw that could allow unauthenticated attackers to execute arbitrary code on self-managed servers under certain conditions. Affected software releases date back a full 12 years - so upgrade to a fixed version now. The integer overflow bug, tracked as CVE-2026-110264 , affects regular-expression compilation in GitLab Community Edition (CE) and Enterprise Edition (EE), including versions dating back to GitLab 7.0, released in June 2014. The flaw, “under certain conditions, could have allowed an unauthenticated user to execute arbitrary code on the GitLab server due to integer overflow when compiling a specially crafted regular expression,” the vendor said in its release notes. GitLab released fixes in versions 19.5.1, 19.4.3, and 19.3.6, and backported the patch to versions 19.2.9, 19.1.9, 19.0.10, and 18.11.13. The vendor “strongly recommends” that all organizations running vulnerable software upgrade to a fixed version “as soon as possible.” GitLab-managed infrastructure, including GitLab.com and GitLab Dedicated, remains patched, and the vendor also released two threat detections ( here and here ) for customers with self-managed instances. Bug hunter Johan Carlsson reported the vulnerability through GitLab’s HackerOne bug bounty program. “For organizations running self-managed GitLab infrastructure, the potential impact is severe,” warned threat-detection firm SOC Prime. “GitLab repositories frequently contain source code, CI/CD configuration, deployment secrets, access tokens, infrastructure definitions, and connections to production environments. Server-level compromise could therefore create opportunities for credential theft, repository manipulation, supply chain attacks, persistence, or lateral movement.” While there’s no indication - yet - of any in-the-wild exploitation attempts, we’d expect criminals to start scanning for vulnerable instances soon. The ongoing PHP chaos may have given defenders a short head-start on this one, but considering the perfect 10 CVSS severity rating and GitLab’s reach into the enterprise - it claims 50 million registered users and more than 50 percent of the Fortune 100 - that’s not going to last long. Last month, attackers started battering another max-severity flaw in the same GitLab CE and EE products just days after the vendor issued a patch, according to the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency and private researchers.®

item.title: Meta shocked by $25B fine after N.M. refused to join multistate settlement
item.description: Meta must pay $25 billion to New Mexico after a jury found the tech giant guilty of nearly 44 million violations of state consumer protection laws. The largest fine to ever hit Meta came after New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez declined to join an $18 billion settlement Meta reached earlier this year with attorneys general in nearly all states. In his opinion Wednesday, US district court judge Francis J. Mathew said there was no “bright line rule” for determining the appropriate penalty for Meta's repeated and willful deception of users since 2010 about their “control of data, third-party data misuse, misinformation, hate speech, and equal enforcement.” Read full article Comments

item.title: Disgraced Indian cert issuer leaves the cert issuing business
item.description: After embarrassing reports revealed weak private keys, one of which was just a single digit, Indian certification authority eMudhra has decided to take the L and get out of the global SSL/TLS cert game entirely. eMudhra announced Thursday that it was abandoning that arm of its business. Sure, the intense scrutiny heaped on the company was a factor, but the firm also argued that growing compliance costs and competition from free certificate providers had made the business increasingly difficult to justify. “Global SSL/TLS is a small part of eMudhra’s business contributing to about 1 percent of the global revenue,” the company explained, noting that free SSL/TLS cert issuance from large firms and increased compliance and data sovereignty requirements have made it a minor part of the firm’s operation, and one that doesn’t merit so much bad press. “The level of social media amplification around this incident has brought scrutiny that is out of proportion to SSL/TLS’s place in our business,” eMudhra explained. “In view of this, after detailed deliberations our board has concluded that withdrawing from global SSL/TLS is the right decision for eMudhra and its shareholders.” An argument could be made that, even if SSL/TLS accounts for just 1 percent of its global revenue, a private CA key with a value of 4 still deserves a thorough public shaming. It’s only been two days since eMudhra’s weak private keys were exposed in public reports , following a report to Mozilla on October 17, and it wasn’t exactly hard for security researchers to recover them: The eight affected private-key values ranged from the number 4 (yes – a plain old number 4), to 56 and 66, to the far more complicated 115, 155, 156, 230, and 237. No quantum computer required to crack those keys. Wow – better save the qubits . This wasn’t just an embarrassing collection of numbers, either: The weak keys belonged to eight intermediate certificate authorities, potentially allowing attackers to forge certificates trusted by systems that hadn’t blocked them. eMudhra, however, maintains that the affected CAs had issued no end-entity certificates. eMudhra quickly went on the defensive about its mind-boggling key-management failure, acknowledging the weak keys while pointing to independent audits and a problem during its key-generation ceremony that it said produced the weak keys alongside the intended strong ones. “A flaw in the key generation ceremony caused a wrap/unwrap step to produce a second set of weak keys alongside the original strong keys,” the company said the day after the key fiasco was reported. “The weak keys were the ones published to the browser root stores.” Despite that, eMudhra said the relevant certificate infrastructure had undergone two years of independent audits and had been in browser trust lists since mid-2025, raising questions about why the weak keys weren't caught sooner. eMudhra claimed on Thursday that the affected CAs had issued no end-entity certificates, that it h
item.dc:creator: Brandon Vigliarolo
item.content:encoded: After embarrassing reports revealed weak private keys, one of which was just a single digit, Indian certification authority eMudhra has decided to take the L and get out of the global SSL/TLS cert game entirely. eMudhra announced Thursday that it was abandoning that arm of its business. Sure, the intense scrutiny heaped on the company was a factor, but the firm also argued that growing compliance costs and competition from free certificate providers had made the business increasingly difficult to justify. “Global SSL/TLS is a small part of eMudhra’s business contributing to about 1 percent of the global revenue,” the company explained, noting that free SSL/TLS cert issuance from large firms and increased compliance and data sovereignty requirements have made it a minor part of the firm’s operation, and one that doesn’t merit so much bad press. “The level of social media amplification around this incident has brought scrutiny that is out of proportion to SSL/TLS’s place in our business,” eMudhra explained. “In view of this, after detailed deliberations our board has concluded that withdrawing from global SSL/TLS is the right decision for eMudhra and its shareholders.” An argument could be made that, even if SSL/TLS accounts for just 1 percent of its global revenue, a private CA key with a value of 4 still deserves a thorough public shaming. It’s only been two days since eMudhra’s weak private keys were exposed in public reports , following a report to Mozilla on October 17, and it wasn’t exactly hard for security researchers to recover them: The eight affected private-key values ranged from the number 4 (yes – a plain old number 4), to 56 and 66, to the far more complicated 115, 155, 156, 230, and 237. No quantum computer required to crack those keys. Wow – better save the qubits . This wasn’t just an embarrassing collection of numbers, either: The weak keys belonged to eight intermediate certificate authorities, potentially allowing attackers to forge certificates trusted by systems that hadn’t blocked them. eMudhra, however, maintains that the affected CAs had issued no end-entity certificates. eMudhra quickly went on the defensive about its mind-boggling key-management failure, acknowledging the weak keys while pointing to independent audits and a problem during its key-generation ceremony that it said produced the weak keys alongside the intended strong ones. “A flaw in the key generation ceremony caused a wrap/unwrap step to produce a second set of weak keys alongside the original strong keys,” the company said the day after the key fiasco was reported. “The weak keys were the ones published to the browser root stores.” Despite that, eMudhra said the relevant certificate infrastructure had undergone two years of independent audits and had been in browser trust lists since mid-2025, raising questions about why the weak keys weren't caught sooner. eMudhra claimed on Thursday that the affected CAs had issued no end-entity certificates, that it had revoked those CAs within 14 hours of discovering the issue, and that neither its infrastructure nor its data had been compromised as a result of its key boo-boo. Still, the incident has given eMudhra another reason to shave off a small part of its business rather than continue facing scrutiny over its certificate operations. It’s still going to issue a root-cause report and fulfill its remaining commitments to browser root programs as it winds down the business. The company said it’ll continue to serve G1 RSA roots until it transitions customers to other certificate issuers, which it will do free of charge. “Revocation and certificate status services will keep running until every issued certificate has expired or been replaced,” the company said. ®

item.title: Websites across world hit by millions of attempts to exploit PHP code flaw
item.description: Problem in language that underpins 70% of sites has led governments and companies to pull sites offline to patch fault Tell us: have you been affected by the PHP code flaw? What is PHP, and how bad is the computer language flaw causing website shutdowns globally ? Websites around the world have been hit by millions of attempts to exploit a recently discovered vulnerability in their code, cybersecurity companies have said, as the US warned the flaw could allow attackers to take control of web servers, steal data and disrupt services. The problem in the PHP programming language, which underpins about 70% of the world’s websites, emerged on Wednesday causing governments and companies to pull their websites off the internet before they could be attacked and so they could patch the fault. Continue reading...

item.title: US-backed vaccine trial on babies canceled after international outcry
item.description: Government officials in Guinea-Bissau have formally rejected a clinical trial that would be run by Danish researchers and funded by the US to look for alleged nonspecific harms from the newborn dose of the hepatitis B vaccine. The vaccine dose is currently recommended globally for all newborns and has been used safely and effectively for decades. In an email to Ars Technica, one of the trial's lead researchers, Christine Stabell Benn of Bandim Health Project and the University of Southern Denmark, said that Guinea-Bissau's Council of Ministers "formally reaffirmed its non-acceptance of the study on 16 October." The revelation that the study was formally rejected last week comes after news on Monday that judicial police in Guinea-Bissau raided Bandim Health's offices and seized vaccines . Stabell Benn highlighted that the police search came after the trial was rejected. Read full article Comments

The lens consists of a reddish elliptical foreground galaxy and the blue arcs of a magnified background galaxy. NASA, ESA, and X. Huang (University of San Francisco); Processing: Gladys Kober (NASA/Catholic University of America) A sweeping barred spiral galaxy marks the spot in this image, but the real treasure is the gravitational lens in the lower-right corner, where a distant background galaxy is being magnified and distorted by the gravity of a closer galaxy. This observation is one of many gravitational lensing images taken by NASA’s Hubble Space Telescope in preparation for science with the new Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope . Gravitational lensing occurs when the mass of a foreground object – such as a galaxy – warps spacetime, causing light to bend, distort, and magnify as it passes around the object, similar to a giant lens in space. Lenses like this occur when a precise chance alignment takes place between the foreground and background galaxies, causing light from the background galaxy to curve around the foreground galaxy. In this image, the gravitational lens features a foreground elliptical galaxy that is about 4.5 billion light-years away. That means the light we see from this galaxy now would have first started traveling toward us when our solar system was still forming. The background galaxy is about eight billion light-years away, almost twice as far. It appears as a pair of arcs, one large and very noticeable to the upper left of the foreground galaxy, the other a much smaller, flipped image of the same background galaxy to the lower right. This configuration is called an arc-counterarc pair. The background galaxy magnified and made visible by this gravitational lens appears twice in this image ― as a large arc and smaller, flipped arc ― on opposite sides of the elliptical foreground galaxy. item.content:encoded: Explore Hubble Hubble Home Overview About Hubble The History of Hubble Hubble Timeline Why Have a Telescope in Space? Hubble by the Numbers At the Museum FAQs Impact & Benefits Hubble’s Impact & Benefits Science Impacts Cultural Impact Technology Benefits Impact on Human Spaceflight Astro Community Impacts Science Hubble Science Science Themes Science Highlights Science Behind Discoveries Universe Uncovered Hubble’s Partners in Science Hubble & Citizen Science SI & Hubble Science Explore the Night Sky Observatory Hubble Observatory Hubble Design Mission Operations Science Operations Astronaut Missions to Hubble Hubble vs. Webb Hubble vs. Roman Team Hubble Team Career Aspirations Hubble Astronauts Multimedia Images Videos Online Activities e-Books Sonifications Podcasts 3D Hubble Models Lithographs Fact Sheets Posters Hubble on the NASA App Glossary News Hubble News Social Media Media Resources 35th Anniversary More Online Activities 4 min read NASA’s Hubble Charts Path for Roman with Gravitational Lenses A sinuous spiral galaxy (center) appears in the same field of view as a vivid gravitational lens (right corner) in this Hubble image. The lens consists of a reddish elliptical foreground galaxy and the blue arcs of a magnified background galaxy. NASA, ESA, and X. Huang (University of San Francisco); Processing: Gladys Kober (NASA/Catholic University of America) A sweeping barred spiral galaxy marks the spot in this image, but the real treasure is the gravitational lens in the lower-right corner, where a distant background galaxy is being magnified and distorted by the gravity of a closer galaxy. This observation is one of many gravitational lensing images taken by NASA’s Hubble Space Telescope in preparation for science with the new Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope . Gravitational lensing occurs when the mass of a foreground object – such as a galaxy – warps spacetime, causing light to bend, distort, and magnify as it passes around the object, similar to a giant lens in space. Lenses like this occur when a precise chance alignment takes place between the foreground and background galaxies, causing light from the background galaxy to curve around the foreground galaxy. In this image, the gravitational lens features a foreground elliptical galaxy that is about 4.5 billion light-years away. That means the light we see from this galaxy now would have first started traveling toward us when our solar system was still forming. The background galaxy is about eight billion light-years away, almost twice as far. It appears as a pair of arcs, one large and very noticeable to the upper left of the foreground galaxy, the other a much smaller, flipped image of the same background galaxy to the lower right. This configuration is called an arc-counterarc pair. The background galaxy magnified and made visible by this gravitational lens appears twice in this image ― as a large arc and smaller, flipped arc ― on opposite sides of the elliptical foreground galaxy. NASA, ESA, and X. Huang (University of San Francisco); Processing: Gladys Kober (NASA/Catholic University of America) The more massive the foreground galaxy is, the stronger the gravitational lens and the more significantly it bends light. By studying the distortion of the background galaxy, researchers can determine how much mass the foreground galaxy contains. This plays a huge role in the study of dark matter, the mysterious, invisible substance that makes up the majority of mass in the universe. The visible matter is not enough to account for the level of distortion in the background galaxy, which allows researchers to calculate both the mass of the foreground galaxy and how much dark matter it contains. Almost all of the objects in this image are galaxies, except for a few scattered foreground stars. The barred spiral galaxy in this image – so called because its arms extend from a bar of stars in its center – is about the size of our own Milky Way galaxy, which astronomers think is a barred spiral as well. The tiny spiral to the left of the large spiral may be a satellite galaxy, similar to the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds that orbit the Milky Way. Hubble views the cosmos primarily in visible and ultraviolet light with some infrared coverage, and Roman sees mainly infrared wavelengths and some visible light. Hubble can provide high-resolution views of individual objects, while Roman has a much larger field of view conducive to panoramas. Images like this offer a glimpse of how Hubble and Roman will work together to build an even more comprehensive picture of the cosmos. This is just one of many gravitational lens images captured by Hubble. Astronomers will use them to analyze gravitational distortions to learn more about dark matter in the foreground galaxies and to lay the groundwork for future Roman observations. Hubble can only view these gravitational lenses one at a time, while Roman’s wide view of the sky will provide a greater sample of these lenses. Astronomers are using Hubble’s sharp images to build a computer model to better analyze dark matter-induced distortions. This tool will help astronomers analyze Roman’s large images. Hubble will also follow up on interesting lenses Roman detects. Facebook logo @NASAHubble @NASAHubble Instagram logo @NASAHubble Explore More Gravitational Lenses Hubble’s Gravitational Lenses Hubble Focus: Gravitational Lenses Media Contact : Claire Andreoli NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center , Greenbelt, MD claire.andreoli@nasa.gov Share Details Last Updated Oct 23, 2026 Editor Andrea Gianopoulos Location NASA Goddard Space Flight Center Related Terms Hubble Space Telescope Astrophysics Astrophysics Division Goddard Space Flight Center Gravitational Lensing Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope The Universe Keep Exploring Discover More Topics From Hubble Hubble Space Telescope Since its 1990 launch, the Hubble Space Telescope has changed our fundamental understanding of the universe. Hubble vs. Roman NASA’s Hubble and Roman space telescopes will work together to broaden our perspective of the universe. Hubble vs. Webb Hubble and Webb observations complement each other, providing us with a broad view of the universe. What Did Hubble See on Your Birthday? Take a look at what cosmic wonders Hubble observed on your special day!

item.title: 'Cabin leak suspected': Artemis II astronaut reveals how a warning nearly derailed NASA's epic moon mission
item.description: null TENERIFE, CANARY ISLANDS — NASA's Artemis II astronauts were just minutes away from a critical engine burn that would send them toward the moon when an unexpected cabin leak warning threatened to change the course of their historic mission. "If it had happened five minutes later, we may not have been able to have that burn," Artemis II pilot Victor Glover revealed during an Oct. 18 discussion with Canadian former astronaut Chris Hadfield at the Starmus VIII festival here in Tenerife. The incident unfolded on April 2, the second day of the Artemis II mission, as the astronauts' Orion spacecraft swooped back toward Earth after traveling some 38,000 miles (61,000 kilometers) away. Orion had been completing a highly elliptical orbit around Earth , giving the crew and mission control an opportunity to test the capsule's systems before committing to the journey to the moon . Orion was now approaching its closest point to our planet, roughly 100 miles (160 km) above the surface, ahead of the crucial translunar injection (TLI) burn that would send the astronauts moonward. "Jeremy looks out the window and says, 'I think we're going to run smack dab into the middle of Earth,'" Glover recalled, referring to Artemis II mission specialist Jeremy Hansen of the Canadian Space Agency . "Because we were getting so low." The close approach brought additional challenges, as Orion passed through a region populated by orbital debris and satellites. "The density of things is going up from where we are, and also an increase in radiation," Glover explained. It was at this particularly demanding point in the mission that Orion issued a warning that indicated a possible cabin leak, around 15 minutes before the critical TLI burn. "So, determining whether it was real or not was a big deal," Glover said. The crew and mission control faced a crucial question: Was it safe to continue heading to the moon , or would they have to abandon the planned maneuver and cut the mission very short? "Are we going to do a TLI and burn to go to the moon, or are we putting on our spacesuits to prepare to come back to Earth right now?" Glover recalled. The timing was particularly critical. The TLI burn was designed to propel Orion out of Earth orbit and onto its trajectory around the moon, marking the first time astronauts had headed toward Earth's nearest neighbor since the Apollo era. The moon, seen here backlit by the sun during a solar eclipse on April 6, 2026, captured by one of the cameras on the Orion spacecraft's solar array wings. (Image credit: NASA) Luckily, as NASA flight director Judd Frieling told us during an April 2 media briefing , the warning turned out to be a false alarm. So Artemis II received the go-ahead. Orion fired its main engine for approximately five minutes and 50 seconds, successfully setting the four astronauts on their journey around the moon. "We're watching the timer count down, velocities go up, and the magenta and green numbers coming together," Glover

Orion had been completing a highly elliptical orbit around Earth , giving the crew and mission control an opportunity to test the capsule's systems before committing to the journey to the moon . Orion was now approaching its closest point to our planet, roughly 100 miles (160 km) above the surface, ahead of the crucial translunar injection (TLI) burn that would send the astronauts moonward. "Jeremy looks out the window and says, 'I think we're going to run smack dab into the middle of Earth,'" Glover recalled, referring to Artemis II mission specialist Jeremy Hansen of the Canadian Space Agency . "Because we were getting so low." The close approach brought additional challenges, as Orion passed through a region populated by orbital debris and satellites. "The density of things is going up from where we are, and also an increase in radiation," Glover explained. It was at this particularly demanding point in the mission that Orion issued a warning that indicated a possible cabin leak, around 15 minutes before the critical TLI burn. "So, determining whether it was real or not was a big deal," Glover said. The crew and mission control faced a crucial question: Was it safe to continue heading to the moon , or would they have to abandon the planned maneuver and cut the mission very short? "Are we going to do a TLI and burn to go to the moon, or are we putting on our spacesuits to prepare to come back to Earth right now?" Glover recalled. The timing was particularly critical. The TLI burn was designed to propel Orion out of Earth orbit and onto its trajectory around the moon, marking the first time astronauts had headed toward Earth's nearest neighbor since the Apollo era. The moon, seen here backlit by the sun during a solar eclipse on April 6, 2026, captured by one of the cameras on the Orion spacecraft's solar array wings. (Image credit: NASA) Luckily, as NASA flight director Judd Frieling told us during an April 2 media briefing , the warning turned out to be a false alarm. So Artemis II received the go-ahead. Orion fired its main engine for approximately five minutes and 50 seconds, successfully setting the four astronauts on their journey around the moon. "We're watching the timer count down, velocities go up, and the magenta and green numbers coming together," Glover recalled. "Everything is tracking. It's looking good." Before long, the crew had broken free of Earth's gravitational hold and were hurtling toward the moon at around 24,500 mph (39,430 kph). Despite the tense moments before the burn, Artemis II went on to make history. NASA astronauts Reid Wiseman (the mission's commander), Glover (pilot) and Christina Koch (mission specialist), along with Hansen, traveled farther from Earth than any humans before them, reaching a maximum distance of 252,756 miles (406,771 km) during their journey around the moon. The four astronauts returned safely to Earth on April 10, splashing down in the Pacific Ocean off the coast of San Diego after nearly 10 days in space.

item.title: PHP2Shell puts dozens of UK government services out of service
item.description: The PHP2Shell security fiasco has forced 32 UK government services offline and left another four partially unavailable as Whitehall scrambles to patch the critical vulnerabilities wreaking havoc across the web. The figures were disclosed in the House of Lords on Thursday, where tech minister Baroness Lloyd of Effra outlined the disruption following the discovery of two critical flaws in PHP . "Currently, the information I have is that 32 government services are unavailable and four are partially unavailable," Lloyd told peers. "That has resulted largely from precautionary measures taken to protect systems while security updates and mitigations are applied." "We are working very carefully with departments to restore the services safely and securely following that remediation activity," she added. Whitehall has not published a full list of affected services, although the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) is among those known to have taken their websites offline, rather inconveniently with next week's Budget looming. Peers also raised reports of disruption affecting the DVLA and police services. Britain isn't alone in pulling the plug. Government websites in Germany, France, Belgium, Finland, and the Netherlands have also been taken offline as a precaution, along with Australia's own cybersecurity agency website. Across the Atlantic, the NSA has urged organizations to patch or disconnect vulnerable systems, although the US government has not publicly confirmed any website shutdowns. PHP2Shell comprises two critical vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, that could allow unauthenticated attackers to execute code on vulnerable servers. The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) warned organizations to patch immediately or consider pulling affected systems offline until they could be fixed. "The NCSC was briefed by OpenAI last week on this potential specific vulnerability and has been working to ensure that disclosure happened in a co-ordinated way with vendors, so there was sufficient preparation to protect customers," Lloyd said. Security firm Calif found one of the PHP bugs using OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol model, while Google's Wiz separately uncovered both flaws with the help of AI tools. OpenAI then dug into the vulnerabilities itself and worked with vendors and government agencies to get the word out. The government established a cross-departmental incident response operation before public disclosure, Lloyd said. The NCSC also sent 50,000 warnings to businesses and other organizations. The disruption has spread beyond central government. Liberal Democrat peer Baroness Ludford pointed to several councils whose services had reportedly been taken offline, including Edinburgh, Oxford, Bristol, Lambeth, and Barnet. She questioned why central government and local authorities remain outside the statutory duties proposed under the government's Cyber Security and Resilience Bill , which returns to the Lords on Monday. "That has resulted largely from precautionary measures taken to protect systems while security updates and mitigations are applied." "We are working very carefully with departments to restore the services safely and securely following that remediation activity," she added. Whitehall has not published a full list of affected services, although the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) is among those known to have taken their websites offline, rather inconveniently with next week's Budget looming. Peers also raised reports of disruption affecting the DVLA and police services. Britain isn't alone in pulling the plug. Across the Atlantic, the NSA has urged organizations to patch or disconnect vulnerable systems, although the US government has not publicly confirmed any website shutdowns. "We are not currently aware of any confirmed compromise of central government systems resulting from these vulnerabilities," Lloyd told peers, later extending that assessment to the wider UK public sector. AWS says attackers were exploiting the flaws four days before they were publicly disclosed , while Cloudflare has since recorded millions of attempts to weaponize them. ®

item.title: This emulator reimagines Nintendo’s Virtual Boy with a full color display
item.description: Last year, we reported on Red Viper , a Virtual Boy emulator that added a splash of Super Game Boy-style color to Nintendo's famously failed red-on-black "portable" 3D headset from the '90s. Now, a new emulation experiment, VBoy Color , has taken the concept to a higher level, using a tile-based palette system that allows for many more distinct colors in each individual Virtual Boy frame. Rather than simply replacing the Virtual Boy's four shades of red with four different colors, VBoy Color's readme files explain how the emulator's game-specific Color Packs can assign a distinct four-color palette to each 8x8 tile in a Virtual Boy scene. That means the emulator can differentiate between green pipes, grey platforms, and red brick wall in Mario Clash , for instance, even though all those in-game objects share the same overlapping red hues in the original game. The Game Boy Color-esque results feel like being transported into an alternate history where Nintendo invested in a full-color display rather than cheaper red LEDs for the Virtual Boy hardware. The increased contrast between differently colored elements is particularly welcome in games like Jack Bros. or Vertical Force , where the original red-on-red display often makes it hard to differentiate the player-character from busy red background elements. Read full article Comments

item.title: Football Daily | Post-Ferguson worn-out horror show continues at Manchester United
item.description: Sign up now! Sign up now! Sign up now? Sign up now! We’re in the midst of what the kids call “spooky season” – or, for our fellow fusty old-timers out there, “autumn”. If you’ve been cosying up with a few horror flicks this month, you’ll know nothing good can come from hanging around a lake at this time of year. And so it proved for Manchester United, who endured an early Halloween nightmare on the banks of Lake Como that may have driven a stake through the Michael Carrick era. Hailed as the interim anti-Amorim not so long ago, Carrick has overseen two wins this season, against Ipswich and Sabah Baku . Como were in Serie D when Carrick won Big Cup with United as a player in 2008 – now, 18 years on, he watched the Italian upstarts dance, twirl and shimmy through the set of training cones he had sent out to represent his storied club. Any chance the Independent Football Regulator could also force the sale of Manchester United while it is at it? – James Marriott. Belated birthday greetings to Florent Sinama-Pongolle, a player once described (by Big Website if memory serves) as the only footballer whose surname sounds like an art-house trend – Alan Burgess. This is an extract from our daily football email … Football Daily. To get the full version, just visit this page and follow the instructions . Continue reading...

item.title: From Nigeria to Tanzania, Meet 5 African Beauty Queens to Know in 2026
item.description: Reigning African beauty queens Jihan Mohin Dimack, Mitchelle Daka, and Tamunosoye Karibi-George. What a year it’s been for African beauty queens. From Nigeria to Tanzania and Uganda, women across the continent are making their mark in pageantry, winning international titles, taking on national crowns and preparing to represent their countries on some of the world’s biggest stages. And there’s so much to know about the women behind these crowns. We’re talking about a medical doctor championing women’s health, a laboratory scientist making history internationally, and advocates using their platforms to support causes they care about. So if you love keeping up with the continent’s brightest trailblazers, these five reigning beauty queens definitely need to be on your radar. Osele Iruomachukwu: Miss Continental World 2026 Osele officially made history by claiming the inaugural title of Miss Continental World 2026 in Ayutthaya, Thailand. When she isn’t serving pure editorial elegance on international runways, she is busy putting her medical laboratory science degree and entrepreneurial background to work. Bringing home a major global win, she is representing Nigeria with serious pride and showing the world what true excellence looks like on the world stage. Osele Iruomachukwu after winning the inaugural Miss Continental World 2026 title in Thailand. item.title: Apple App Store review process hits a traffic jam
item.description: Whatever the task, there's an app for that… Except for the process of reviewing those apps, apparently. There are a growing number of reports on Apple's developer forums that developers are waiting a long time for their apps to be reviewed before they’re listed on the App Store. Subjects include 'Unusually long Apple 'waiting for review' time", "Stuck in Waiting for Review for about 3 weeks", "Stuck in 'Waiting for Review' since October 8", and so on, including a "Waiting for Review Megathread." To pick an example at random, D1 Tech say they've been waiting since September 19 . There are also reports on Reddit, such as " My app has been waiting for App Store review for almost a month. Is this normal? " The typical review time is a day or two. Apple's own App Review guidelines say: App Review works around the clock, typically reviewing at least 50% of submissions in less than 24 hours and 90% in less than 48 hours." This isn't the first time this has happened. A thread of similar complaints is still visible from back in February, with at least 74 developers complaining of multi-week delays. Some of them noted that these were not new app submissions, but merely bug-fixes for existing, approved apps. In March, Business Insider reported on similar delays, suggesting that it was due to a large and rising influx of AI-coded apps. In April, The Information reported that submissions were up 84 percent. We have asked Apple if it has any explanation or comment to make about the delay. So far, the company has not replied, but we will update this story if we receive any more information. Saying that, though, long-term readers of The Register may remember vulture Kieren McCarthy’s three-month effort to attend Apple's iPhone 7 launch party , a decade ago. (Spoiler: he did not, in fact, get to join the party.) It is just conceivable that El Reg is not Cupertino's favorite news outlet. ®

item.title: When the attacker becomes the user: Rethinking account takeover
item.description: In a world full of cyber risk, account takeover has emerged as one of the most insidious of all threats. If an attacker can successfully compromise a legitimate email account, they are then able to pose as a trusted individual or organization without triggering any warnings. Traditional email security will see nothing wrong. From there the threat actor can pick their moment to cause havoc with objectives that range from stealing money, expropriating sensitive data and propagating catastrophic malware. Serious financial loss and a damaged corporate reputation are commonplace outcomes. The typical account takeover lifecycle starts with the bad guys obtaining credentials, usually through the medium of phishing. Generative AI (GenAI) has made it easy for an attacker to trick an unwary individual into giving away login data, perhaps by posing as a colleague or other trusted party or by encouraging them to enter confidential information on a fake login page. You might expect, once a legitimate identity has been successfully compromised, that all hell would immediately break loose. These days the typical account takeover artist is more stealthy and sinister than that, in no rush to act at this early stage since no alarm bells have been triggered. Most will take their time to test out and verify their stolen login data, and see where it might take them. “Conventionally attackers would take over an account and immediately start firing off spam and phishing,” says Dave Baggett, SVP Cybersecurity with software developer Kaseya. “Now they are starting to get clever. They’ll get access to an account and sit tight, watching all the email traffic passing and waiting for an opportune moment to inject themselves into the conversation.” From the inside out Once they’ve figured out an organisation’s weak points and come up with a plan of attack, the bad guys will start to weaponize the compromised email account to target other employees and internal systems. Assuming their motivation is financial, they might be on the hunt for a way into payroll or invoicing databases. But their ultimate aim might lie further afield in the form of the organisation’s customers and suppliers, and that’s when the real nightmare can start. So called outbound phishing offers the criminal a way to assert control over a whole new range of sensitive end points. Victims of outbound phishing are highly vulnerable in the face of what seem to be messages from a trusted partner and ally. It is one thing for an organisation to protect its own email accounts with robust controls like multifactor authentication (MFA), but no one has control over the authentication practices of other parties: “Let’s say we have a customer who we’re protecting,” explains Baggett. “They’re safe, but imagine that they start getting suspicious emails from a third party. Our customer has no idea what is or isn’t protecting that third party. Emails coming from that source might appear to be from a real account, but it co
item.dc:creator: Guy Matthews
item.content:encoded: In a world full of cyber risk, account takeover has emerged as one of the most insidious of all threats. If an attacker can successfully compromise a legitimate email account, they are then able to pose as a trusted individual or organization without triggering any warnings. Traditional email security will see nothing wrong. From there the threat actor can pick their moment to cause havoc with objectives that range from stealing money, expropriating sensitive data and propagating catastrophic malware. Serious financial loss and a damaged corporate reputation are commonplace outcomes. The typical account takeover lifecycle starts with the bad guys obtaining credentials, usually through the medium of phishing. Generative AI (GenAI) has made it easy for an attacker to trick an unwary individual into giving away login data, perhaps by posing as a colleague or other trusted party or by encouraging them to enter confidential information on a fake login page. You might expect, once a legitimate identity has been successfully compromised, that all hell would immediately break loose. These days the typical account takeover artist is more stealthy and sinister than that, in no rush to act at this early stage since no alarm bells have been triggered. Most will take their time to test out and verify their stolen login data, and see where it might take them. “Conventionally attackers would take over an account and immediately start firing off spam and phishing,” says Dave Baggett, SVP Cybersecurity with software developer Kaseya. “Now they are starting to get clever. They’ll get access to an account and sit tight, watching all the email traffic passing and waiting for an opportune moment to inject themselves into the conversation.” From the inside out Once they’ve figured out an organisation’s weak points and come up with a plan of attack, the bad guys will start to weaponize the compromised email account to target other employees and internal systems. Assuming their motivation is financial, they might be on the hunt for a way into payroll or invoicing databases. But their ultimate aim might lie further afield in the form of the organisation’s customers and suppliers, and that’s when the real nightmare can start. So called outbound phishing offers the criminal a way to assert control over a whole new range of sensitive end points. Victims of outbound phishing are highly vulnerable in the face of what seem to be messages from a trusted partner and ally. It is one thing for an organisation to protect its own email accounts with robust controls like multifactor authentication (MFA), but no one has control over the authentication practices of other parties: “Let’s say we have a customer who we’re protecting,” explains Baggett. “They’re safe, but imagine that they start getting suspicious emails from a third party. Our customer has no idea what is or isn’t protecting that third party. Emails coming from that source might appear to be from a real account, but it could be a hacker typing them.” Given that you can’t run checks on third party organisations, something more sophisticated than regular email security is required. Ideally this would be a GenAI-powered solution that can bring language understanding to bear, able to examine conversation histories in depth to see if something anomalous can be spotted. It makes life even harder for defenders when the bad actor has successfully assumed the identity of somebody senior. If they are impersonating a top-tier manager with an extensive and trusted reputation then they have a powerful asset on their hands. All the trust and goodwill of that senior individual is now inherited by the criminal. Conventional email filtering systems will often be configured to allow senior personnel past certain defensive layers with minimal friction, so as not to restrict important business communications. Recipients of mail from such sources may be disinclined to challenge and report them, should suspicions be raised by the nature of what they are asking for. It takes a bold employee to call out as fraud what seems to be a message from somebody at C-level, especially when the email system has apparently green lighted it as authentic. Bringing the power of AI to bear The heat is on not just for IT departments but for MSPs who have multiple organisations under their protection, many of which will have no real in-house security knowledge of their own. Kaseya’s own research shows just how exposed many are . New approaches are needed that deal with the menace of account takeover before damage can be caused. And should a takeover transpire, consideration must be given to containing its impact before vital data and infrastructure are affected. The good news is that modern tools exist that perform just these tasks. INKY is Kaseya's generative AI-driven email analysis tool. It has capabilities that go well beyond any kind of traditional email security, tuned to detect, through the most subtle and marginal signs, when an email conversation is in the process of being infiltrated. Using techniques such as advanced sender profiling, stylometry and machine learning, INKY is adept at identifying inconsistencies between the known writing patterns of a legitimate employee and the slightly unfamiliar tone of a fake message. It can sniff out that something is wrong, even when message headers seem real, just by spotting the kind of contextual anomalies that expose a phoney message. INKY is especially useful when it comes to third party account takeover. It achieves this by building and maintaining detailed profiles of trusted senders based on technical and behavioural characteristics. Over time it learns what “normal” looks like and can see when a third-party email doesn’t match a sender’s established profile. Containing an attack If a takeover attempt has been successful, there’s more to stemming the damage than just putting a block on a suspect account. By the time of its discovery, a compromised identity may have already led to inroads being made into connected SaaS apps, cloud storage and collaboration tools, widening the possible blast zone well beyond a single email thread. Modern IT environments are a jungle of identity-driven endpoints and gateways, and therefore increasingly difficult to defend against intruders armed with legitimate credentials. To compound matters, when the bad guys have AI at their disposal they are able to treat these SaaS-driven ecosystems as a single attack surface. Defence that relies on a patchwork of individual tools, each created to solve a particular challenge in one silo of the organisation, will not be up to countering this kind of threat. That’s why INKY is configured to work with Kaseya SaaS Alerts, a cloud-based detection and response platform designed to help MSPs and others to monitor and protect business applications. Once INKY has picked up that a mailbox has been hijacked, it isolates the user and blocks outbound mail. It then sends an event to SaaS Alerts so that it can lock down that user's access across the rest of the stack. The tools work as a team, INKY blocking the compromised account and SaaS Alerts preventing the damage from spreading. The power of this partnership comes from INKY’s ability to stream real-time email security telemetry into SaaS Alerts, including inbound analysis results and threat detections, user-reported phishing activity and outbound mail protection events. This type of integration helps to automate real-time threat detection across a complex SaaS ecosystem. “It means if we see suspicious mail going out, we can shut the account down, and take other remedial actions,” says Baggett. “The more you understand the meaning of the mail, the more you can catch.” Smart tools to the rescue The battle against account takeover is never won, and future innovation is always needed. We’ve seen how AI is a dangerous weapon in the hands of the attacker. It’s also a very handy tool fo

item.title: Sauron recruits his future Ringwraiths in Rings of Power S3 trailer
item.description: Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power returns next month for its third season. Prime Video unveiled a teaser earlier this year at San Diego Comic-Con, but we haven't heard much about the new season otherwise. We now have the official full trailer, and it's jam-packed with a rising Sauron, who is intent on conquering Middle-Earth with his army of Orcs—with the fractured opposition of elves, dwarves, and men scrambling to figure out how best to stop him. We also meet the human men who will become the Ringwraiths; the showrunners have dubbed them the Nazgnagol ("Rings-servant"). (Some spoilers for the first two seasons below.) Prime Video made a major investment in The Rings of Power when it acquired the rights to the source material from the Tolkien estate, even committing to multiple seasons upfront. S3 is set seven years after the events of S2 and opens when the war between the elves and Sauron is at its height. Per the official synopsis: Read full article Comments

item.title: Singapore boffins weave a GUI into fabric, and it's machine washable too
item.description: Researchers in Singapore have developed an electronic fabric they claim can be woven into garments to create a new form of graphical user interface (GUI), for people who find retrieving a device from their pocket too much effort. The development could lead - at some point - to a "future in which clothing functions as a pervasive, multimodal human–computer interface," according to the study published in peer-reviewed science journal Nature this week. The paper shows someone interacting with computing devices using the sleeve of a wool sweater (no jokes about the Windows ugly sweater please, this is serious). The researchers, led by Singapore National University research engineer Fu Heng, claim this is a big leap forward. “This fiber-centric approach shifts wearable electronics from flexible panels toward truly textile-native architectures, laying the groundwork for fabrics that visualize, sense, communicate and compute as naturally as the garments they inhabit,” the paper says. The researchers claim to have developed a scalable process to make millimeter-thick fibers. Using lasers to strip the insulation from specific spots on the thin copper wires, they attached light-emitting chips to the exposed sections, creating electrical connections to the chips. Thousands of chips were connected to the wires with extreme precision using this process. The fibers were then fed into a transparent plastic tube, and made pressure-sensitive by adding two strips of a compressible, conductive polymer into a second longitudinal channel in the tube. The paper says they could make fibers 10 meters long using this method, and that they are thin and flexible enough to be woven into or attached to fabrics. The researchers were also able to add "peripherals" such as a microphone, a speaker, a temperature sensor and a light sensor. The researchers reckon they could build into the sleeve of a sweater an interactive interface with audio-video playback, wireless data exchange, computing, and dynamic graphics. The fabric can survive 50 gentle machine washes and 1,000 bending cycles without losing its functionality, we're told. In an accompanying article, Shanshan Yao, assistant professor at the Department of Mechanical Engineering, Stony Brook University, said the main advance lay in building functionality directly into fiber, which were then assembled into a fabric. “If the fibers prove to be compatible with standard industrial weaving, knitting and embroidery processes, the findings would pave the way to producing multifunctional electronic textiles in almost any shape or size,” she said. "The work is also a big step towards replacing rigid displays with fully integrated wearable interfaces, moving everyday computing away from flat screens to fabrics that comfortably conform to the human body. The interactive features of the GUI that have been demonstrated so far are relatively simple, comparable to those of early-generation smartphones and tablets," she said. However, the

The development could lead - at some point - to a "future in which clothing functions as a pervasive, multimodal human–computer interface," according to the study published in peer-reviewed science journal Nature this week. The paper shows someone interacting with computing devices using the sleeve of a wool sweater (no jokes about the Windows ugly sweater please, this is serious). The researchers, led by Singapore National University research engineer Fu Heng, claim this is a big leap forward. “This fiber-centric approach shifts wearable electronics from flexible panels toward truly textile-native architectures, laying the groundwork for fabrics that visualize, sense, communicate and compute as naturally as the garments they inhabit,” the paper says. The researchers claim to have developed a scalable process to make millimeter-thick fibers. Using lasers to strip the insulation from specific spots on the thin copper wires, they attached light-emitting chips to the exposed sections, creating electrical connections to the chips. Thousands of chips were connected to the wires with extreme precision using this process. The fibers were then fed into a transparent plastic tube, and made pressure-sensitive by adding two strips of a compressible, conductive polymer into a second longitudinal channel in the tube. The paper says they could make fibers 10 meters long using this method, and that they are thin and flexible enough to be woven into or attached to fabrics. The researchers were also able to add "peripherals" such as a microphone, a speaker, a temperature sensor and a light sensor. The researchers reckon they could build into the sleeve of a sweater an interactive interface with audio-video playback, wireless data exchange, computing, and dynamic graphics. The fabric can survive 50 gentle machine washes and 1,000 bending cycles without losing its functionality, we're told. In an accompanying article, Shanshan Yao, assistant professor at the Department of Mechanical Engineering, Stony Brook University, said the main advance lay in building functionality directly into fiber, which were then assembled into a fabric. “If the fibers prove to be compatible with standard industrial weaving, knitting and embroidery processes, the findings would pave the way to producing multifunctional electronic textiles in almost any shape or size,” she said. "The work is also a big step towards replacing rigid displays with fully integrated wearable interfaces, moving everyday computing away from flat screens to fabrics that comfortably conform to the human body. The interactive features of the GUI that have been demonstrated so far are relatively simple, comparable to those of early-generation smartphones and tablets," she said. However, the current prototype relies on separate microcontroller circuits connected to the fibers through cables, and external battery packs to supply power, she pointed out. "Future research should focus on integrating the control electronics more seamlessly to improve wearability, and on integrating flexible, energy-harvesting threads that can generate power from body heat or movement," she added. ®

item.title: Australia's bizarre 'Spider Crater' seen from orbit | Space photo of the day for Oct. 22, 2026
item.description: null A satellite image of "Spider Crater" in Western Australia. (Image credit: NASA Earth Observatory image by Michala Garrison, using Landsat data from the U.S. Geological Survey ) From the dangerous Sydney funnel-web to the common huntsman, Australia is home to its fair share of spiders. It even has a crater shaped like one. What is it? One stretch of the vast Western Australia wilderness is imprinted with a curious crater, which likely formed after a meteor impact hundreds of millions of years ago. Geologists think the spider-like pattern in the crater's center was created when its floor rebounded following the initial impact, NASA has said . In the hundreds of millions of years since the initial impact, erosion has continued to carve this formation into its current, signature shape. Complete with "legs," the planetary imprint has earned its name Spider Crater. This image shows the impact structure in its entirety, which stretches 8 by 7 miles (13 by 11 kilometers) in full, with the central "spider" piece measuring 2.5 miles (4 km). Why is it incredible? In this image, we can see this "spider" from space. This snapshot shows the geologic feature as captured by the OLI (Operational Land Imager) aboard the Landsat 9 satellite , an Earth-observing craft that launched back in 2021. The satellite, a collaborative effort between NASA and the U.S. Geological Survey, is the ninth in the Landsat Earth-observing series, which goes all the way back to the launch of Landsat 1 in 1972. On a near-weekly basis, Landsat 9 delivers observations of everything from deforestation to water quality and crop growth. The series of Landsat satellites have been a critical piece in the modern understanding of how our planet continues to change. Whether it's the repercussions of climate change or fluctuations in agriculture, observations from orbit do more than provide interesting photos of our home world; they also capture critical data.

item.title: Champions League review: PSG take a hit, Man City’s empty seats and teenage hope for Liverpool
item.description: The reigning champions must deal with the absence of Khvicha Kvaratskhelia for some time, while fans at Anfield were thrilled by Rio Ngumoha Paris Saint-Germain beat Barcelona 4-2 on Tuesday , but the reigning champions lost the best player in last season’s tournament, Khvicha Kvaratskhelia. This autumn has seen much lobbying for the Ballon d’Or, with the Georgian a popular choice, despite his absence from the World Cup. He is expected to be out for six months, although Rodri’s comeback from serious injury – he was rested by Barcelona on Tuesday until coming off the bench in the 60th minute – shows it can take far longer than that for players to rediscover their highest level. Continue reading...

item.title: Nvidia's Huang: Don't mention the AI-pocalypse
item.description: Jensen Huang wants the world to stop fretting about AI and start building with it. At Nvidia's GTC event in Berlin, he dismissed predictions of human extinction, defended AI's job prospects, and pitched a $4,000 computer as the family robot. The Nvidia chief's relentless optimism occasionally gave way to irritation during a question-and-answer session. "If we don't describe a future worthy to be part of, then we're not going to lead people there," he said. "We have to describe a future worthy of creating. We have to describe a future not of fear, but of optimism. Who wants to create a future that's worse than today's? We don't have to work hard to create a future worse than today. We just let it happen, isn't that right?" Huang said that we still have to ask the hard questions about safety and jobs, but "it's important, of course, that we don't make it up. It is not helpful in describing an optimistic future when you say that it will be the end of the human civilization. First of all, it's not true. It's made up. I know it gets headlines," he said, dismissing such stories as clickbait. When asked if AI really makes people more productive, he explained that there are two ways to think about that: either it helps you do the same old thing more efficiently, or it helps you do things you couldn't before. "Most of engineering, most of design, has to do with exploring options. Try, experiment, try and experiment, iterate, experiment, iterate," he said. "What's the best combination? And you can only have so much time to try different versions. Now I have AI to go off and explore that universe. That is productivity. And inside our company, we do this every single day now. We're exploring the universe of design options that are within the constraints that we care about, that are physical or realistic constraints." Huang pointed to construction and infrastructure work generated by the AI datacenter boom. "Construction workers, plumbers, electricians, networking engineers, all of those incredible jobs are being created in the United States. I think it already has created a million jobs, and then the layer above that, look at all the startups that are being created," he claimed. "That's productivity, increasing the GDP, increasing our growth, which also results in increasing how busy we are. But that's the end. AI makes jobs, and hopefully doesn't take jobs." Asked about people already losing work to AI - global financial services group Barclays Bank said only this morning it is chopping 5,000 workers and relying more on AI - Huang argued that technological change has always displaced some jobs while creating others. "Now, with AI, of course, some jobs are not necessary as much as before, or maybe not as interesting as before. And some new jobs and new companies and new businesses are necessary. "Most of engineering, most of design, has to do with exploring options. Try, experiment, try and experiment, iterate, experiment, iterate," he said. "What's the best combination? And you can only have so much time to try different versions. Now I have AI to go off and explore that universe. That is productivity. And inside our company, we do this every single day now. We're exploring the universe of design options that are within the constraints that we care about, that are physical or realistic constraints." Huang pointed to construction and infrastructure work generated by the AI datacenter boom. "Construction workers, plumbers, electricians, networking engineers, all of those incredible jobs are being created in the United States. I think it already has created a million jobs, and then the layer above that, look at all the startups that are being created," he claimed. "That's productivity, increasing the GDP, increasing our growth, which also results in increasing how busy we are. But that's the end. AI makes jobs, and hopefully doesn't take jobs." Asked about people already losing work to AI - global financial services group Barclays Bank said only this morning it is chopping 5,000 workers and relying more on AI - Huang argued that technological change has always displaced some jobs while creating others. "Now, with AI, of course, some jobs are not necessary as much as before, or maybe not as interesting as before. And some new jobs and new companies and new businesses are necessary. It's the nature of the world," he stated. On safety, Huang pointed to Nvidia's OpenShell sandbox technology, designed to restrict agents to the resources needed for a task. "If you're making an omelette, you don't need a hammer," he said. But he got hot under the collar when asked about slowing down the pace of AI development while the risks were evaluated, in light of incidents such as AI agents from Anthropic and OpenAI breaking into other computer systems. "You would favor pacing the frontier? I favor them doing whatever they need to do to not bring harm to society," Huang said. "You, sir, if you believe that you should not leave your house because you're inappropriately dressed, or somehow you're going to bring harm to society, could you please not come out?" he told the questioner. "The message from the labs is that there's a collective action problem, and that some minimum standards in coordination would be good here. That's a different question. If you know something is already delivering harm, you got to stop running," he added. Nvidia has a commercial interest in keeping the AI build-out moving. It reported $215.9 billion in revenue for fiscal 2026 and $120 billion in net profit. In the first half of its fiscal 2027, those net profits were already close to the prior year's . The opportunity isn't limited to just chips either. Huang put the price of licensing Nvidia's software stack at about $2,000 per GPU annually. The CEO's domestic vision was also on show. Asked when households could run large AI models, he held up a DGX Spark system. "This computer has a chip called N1X inside, and N1X has 128 gigabytes of memory… It's $4,000. You're right. It's quite expensive. However, that computer was designed to sit on the network in your house, and it would have agents that are used by all of your family members. So it's kind of like a TV. It's sitting in your house. It's shared by everyone, and everybody's agents will be running on DGX Spark," he explained. As an example, Huang said his home agent had researched Berlin's best schnitzel and produced a brochure with restaurant pictures and menus. "So that agent, you know, that computer will become essentially your family's robot. It has no arms and legs, but it's an agent, so it's kind of like a robot. And this one is just for your home. So that's kind of how I see the future. This is pretty affordable. This is a personal computer." Affordable if your net worth is around $180-$190 billion. Maybe not to the average household struggling to pay bills in a cost of living crisis. ®

item.title: Cardi B Makes Her Tiny Desk Debut With “Bodak Yellow,” “Be Careful” & More | Watch
item.description: Autographed polaroid photo of Cardi B at the NPR Music office for her Tiny Desk Concert set. Photo Credit: NPR Music/Instagram If you thought you knew what a Cardi B live set looked like, think again. The rap superstar recently stepped into the NPR Music office for her debut Tiny Desk Concert, and the atmosphere was nothing short of electric. Word got out fast, drawing one of the biggest crowds the office has ever seen as people from all walks of life lined up to watch hip-hop’s most unfiltered star take over the iconic workspace. Dressed sharply in leather trousers and a power blazer, Cardi brought a refreshingly humble and humorous spirit to the desk, delivering a masterclass in stage presence. Kicking things off with the haunting synths and outright confidence of “ Hello ,” she immediately set the tone before riding that unstoppable energy into a reimagined version of “ ErrTime .” Never one to shy away from versatility, she then shifted gears into deeply personal material, performing the vulnerable “ Man of Your Word ” and “ Be Careful ” while keeping her trademark wit and humor intact. “Change the vibes, change the vibes,” she joked with a smile, before bringing the ultimate party back with “ Up ,” which slid straight into “ AH HA .” To close out the unforgettable set, she treated the packed room to two pivotal anthems from her legendary catalogue: “ Bodak Yellow ,” the breakout hit that started it all, and the boogaloo-heavy crowd-pleaser “ I Like It .” By the end of the set, Cardi was swinging her hips right along with the ecstatic crowd, leaving the room beaming with gratitude and handing out warm hugs to a few lucky audience members. It is safe to say the Desk has never seen anything quite like it. Watch below The post Cardi B Makes Her Tiny Desk Debut With “Bodak Yellow,” “Be Careful” & More | Watch appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. Read today! .

item.title: ‘The tech bro fight club is real!’ The titans of AI get the Succession treatment in a wild new TV show
item.description: The Audacity is a fearless satire taking on Silicon Valley’s ‘egomaniac weirdos’. Its creator and stars talk ayahuasca ceremonies, mining kids for data – and punching CEOs Showrunner Jonathan Glatzer wanted the tagline of his latest TV creation to be: “We’re so fucked.” He laughs. “Sadly it got rejected by the network. Hey, maybe I can use it for season two!” The show in question is The Audacity, his darkly comic drama about AI tech titans. Instead, it went with the more PG tagline “Move fast and break people” – a twist on “Move fast and break things”, the Facebook motto coined by Mark Zuckerberg. The Audacity promises to do for tech bros what Succession did for legacy media. Considering Glatzer is a former writer on Succession, that is no empty threat. This acerbic and all-too-timely Silicon Valley satire follows CEO Duncan Park (played by Billy Magnussen), the obscenely wealthy founder of a data analytics company. He’s a self-proclaimed “inventor of the future” who also happens to be a morally bankrupt man-baby. “Duncan is worth about half a billion,” says Glatzer. “Naturally, that’s not enough. He desperately wants to be a billionaire and ascend to what we call ‘God Mountain’. But he’s no God.” Continue reading...
